projects.tagline: Open-source (GPL-3.0) Android app to read, listen to and remember books
projects._verify: Resumes earlier claimed GitHub Actions CI and signed APK releases; the README does not show either, so they are left out until the workflow exists.

story.hook: my open-source (GPL-3.0) Android app for reading, listening to and remembering books, which I designed and built alone in Kotlin and Jetpack Compose
story.contribution: The architecture is mine end to end: app, core, engine and feature modules covering the reader, the narration engine, the AI features and the spaced-repetition scheduler
story.hard_problem: keeping everything anchored to the text, because bookmarks, highlights, audio sync and flashcards all break when a book re-paginates
story.solution: a Text Spine of deterministic sentence and paragraph IDs that every feature shares as one coordinate system
story.verification: Each module has its own unit tests that run through Gradle, so a regression in the EPUB, TTS, playback, AI or spaced-repetition engines shows up before it reaches the app. Because a highlight, bookmark or audio position is just a deterministic Text Spine ID, I can change the typography, re-paginate, and confirm each one still lands on the same sentence. The AI Fence is enforced where the prompt is assembled, not by asking the model to behave, so verifying it means inspecting the assembled context and confirming nothing past the reading position is in it.
highlights: Narration runs through a Media3 read-along player with sentence-level highlighting, using offline system TTS or Fish Audio neural voices, with long chapters generated in the background by WorkManager.
An AI Fence clips every LLM prompt (OpenRouter, bring your own key) to the reader's current position, so chapter summaries and recaps never spoil unread chapters.
Search runs on SQLite FTS5 over a Readium 3.4 EPUB reader, and reviews use FSRS-6 spaced repetition.
Privacy is built in: no telemetry, and API keys are encrypted with Android Keystore AES-256-GCM.
The code is split into app, core, engine and feature modules, and each module has its own unit tests run through Gradle.
